title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
Welcome
This website contains materials for MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra (3 units, GE Area 2) at Cal Poly Humboldt. Class meets face to face Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, 10:00–10:50 a.m., in FR 201.
Catalog description: Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
This site follows three units: representing and comparing things with vectors; transforming, solving, simulating, and computing with matrices; then explaining dynamics, fitting data, and exploiting structure (eigenvectors, least squares, SVD). Daily learning objectives are on Lectures. Class outlines for later meetings will be posted before those days.

title: MATH 107: Introduction to Linear Algebra
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily objectives for each meeting are on the lectures page.

title: Lab 2 — Finding Similar Things (software)
text:
Exercises
Pick Octave or Python for the term.
E1. Lab 1 recall. Query \(x=(2,1)\) and candidates as rows of \[
Z=\begin{bmatrix}2&2\\0&1\\3&1\\2&0\\1.5&1.5\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute all five distances and the nearest index. Confirm against Lab 1 expected values (\(1,\ 2,\ 1,\ 1,\ \sqrt{1/2}\); nearest \(z_5\)).
Octave:
x = [2; 1];
Z = [2 2; 0 1; 3 1; 2 0; 1.5 1.5];
d = sqrt(sum((Z - x').^2, 2))
[~, j] = min(d)   % 1-based
Python:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([2.0, 1.0])
Z = np.array([[2, 2], [0, 1], [3, 1], [2, 0], [1.5, 1.5]])
d = np.linalg.norm(Z - x, axis=1)
j = np.argmin(d)   # 0-based
E2. Rescale. Multiply the first feature of \(x\) and every row of \(Z\) by \(10\). Recompute the nearest neighbor(s). Did the answer change?
Expected: tie between \(z_1\) and \(z_4\); yes, changed.
E3. Slightly larger set. Six “song” feature vectors (energy, danceability), one per row:
0.2  0.1
0.3  0.2
0.25 0.15
0.9  0.8
0.85 0.9
0.95 0.75
Query \(x=(0.28, 0.18)\). Find the nearest neighbor. By eye, which group (low-energy vs high-energy) does \(x\) belong with?
E4 (stretch). One \(k\)-means assignment. Representatives \(z_1=(0.25,0.15)\), \(z_2=(0.9,0.8)\). Assign each of the six songs to the nearer representative. List the two clusters by row number (1-based).
E5 (stretch). Cosine vs distance. For \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(10,0.1)\), compute \(\lVert a-b\rVert\) and the cosine similarity. In one sentence: which comparison treats them as “more similar,” and why might that matter for documents?

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, students should be able to:

Recognize simple dependent and independent collections.
Construct a dependence relationship.
Interpret dependence as redundant information.
Explain why redundancy matters in data, measurement, and computation.

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\), \(b=(0,1)\), and \(c=(1,1)\).

Find scalars \(\alpha,\beta\) (not both zero is fine) so that \(c=\alpha a+\beta b\).
In one sentence: is knowing \(c\) “new information” once you already know \(a\) and \(b\)?

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Fill in
A list of \(n\)-vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) is linearly dependent if there exist scalars \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k\), not all zero, such that \[
\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k = \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}.
\] Any such nontrivial combination equal to zero is a dependence relation.
The list is linearly independent if the only solution of \(\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k=0\) is \(\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_k=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
Equivalent picture: the list is dependent if (and only if) at least one vector is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the others (or the list contains the zero vector).
Redundancy: if the vectors are features, sensors, or columns of data and they are dependent, then at least one measurement can be \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) from the others — it does not add a new independent piece of information.
A single nonzero vector is always \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\). Two vectors are dependent iff one is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of the other.

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Worked in class
W1. Independent or dependent? For each list in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), decide and give a one-line reason.

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((2,4),\ (1,2)\)
\((1,1),\ (1,-1),\ (0,2)\)

W2. Construct a dependence relation. For \(u=(1,2)\), \(v=(2,1)\), \(w=(3,3)\), find \(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3\) not all zero with \(\beta_1 u+\beta_2 v+\beta_3 w=0\). (Hint: notice \(w=u+v\).)
W3. Sensors. Three temperature sensors report daily averages as vectors of length \(7\). Sensor C always equals (Sensor A \(+\) Sensor B)\(/2\). Are the three weekly report vectors dependent? What does that mean for “how many independent sensors” you really have?
W4. Features. Customer vectors (age, income, spending). Someone adds a fourth feature “age in months” \(=12\times\) age. Does the new feature add independent information for linear models that use these coordinates?
W5. Zero vector. Why is any list that includes \(0\) automatically dependent?

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Check yourself
C1. Are \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\), \((0,0,1)\) independent in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)? Brief reason.
C2. Find a dependence relation for \((1,1)\), \((2,2)\), \((0,1)\).
C3. True or false: if every pair in a list of three vectors is independent, then the whole list is independent.
C4. In one sentence: why might redundant features waste storage or confuse nearest-neighbor distance?
C5. Give one independent list of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and one dependent list of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. Yes. If \(\beta_1(1,0,0)+\beta_2(0,1,0)+\beta_3(0,0,1)=0\), then \((\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)=0\), so only the trivial combination works.
C2. Example: \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\) are multiples, so \(2\cdot(1,1)+(-1)\cdot(2,2)+0\cdot(0,1)=0\). (Any nontrivial relation that uses that fact is fine.)
C3. False. Counterexample: \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\), \((1,1)\) — each pair is independent, but the three are dependent because \((1,1)=(1,0)+(0,1)\).
C4. A redundant coordinate can overweight that direction in Euclidean distance (or store duplicated information) without adding a new independent signal.
C5. Independent example: \((1,0),\ (0,1)\). Dependent example: \((1,2),\ (2,4)\).

text:

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(0,1)\). Can you write \(v=(3,-2)\) as \(\alpha a+\beta b\)? If yes, give \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Fill in
The span of vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) is the set of all linear combinations \[
\operatorname{span}\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}
  = \{\, \beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k \mid \beta_i\in\mathbb{R} \,\}.
\] So \(v\) lies in the span iff the equation \(\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k=v\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
Geometry (in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) or \(\mathbb{R}^3\)):

Span of one nonzero vector: a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) through the origin.
Span of two non-parallel vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) through the origin.
Span of the standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\): all of \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).

A subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty set \(V\) closed under addition and scalar multiplication (equivalently: closed under linear combinations). Every subspace contains \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
Spans are always subspaces. A line or plane that does not pass through the origin is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) a subspace (it fails to contain \(0\), or fails closure under scaling).
Independence vs span: an independent list that spans \(V\) will be called a basis of \(V\) next class. Today, focus on “can I build \(v\) from these vectors?”

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Worked in class
W1. Membership. Let \(a=(1,1)\) and \(b=(1,-1)\).

Is \(v=(2,0)\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\)? Find coefficients or explain why not.
Is \(w=(1,0,0)\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)\}\) inside \(\mathbb{R}^3\)?

W2. Geometry. Sketch in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \(\operatorname{span}\{(2,1)\}\) and \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\).
W3. Subspace check. Which of the following are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)? Brief reason.

All vectors \((x,y)\) with \(y=3x\).
All vectors \((x,y)\) with \(y=3x+1\).
The single point \(\{(0,0)\}\).
All vectors with \(\lVert(x,y)\rVert=1\) (the unit circle).

W4. Dependent generators. Let \(a=(1,0)\), \(b=(2,0)\), \(c=(0,1)\). Explain why \(\operatorname{span}\{a,b,c\}=\operatorname{span}\{a,c\}\). What does that say about redundant generators?
W5. Application. Two feature directions \(f_1=\)“morning temperature pattern” and \(f_2=\)“afternoon pattern” as \(24\)-vectors. What does it mean if a third pattern \(g\) lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{f_1,f_2\}\)?

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Check yourself
C1. Complete: \(v\in\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\) means \(v=\underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}\) for some scalars.
C2. Is \((3,3)\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,1)\}\)? Coefficients if yes.
C3. True or false: every subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a span of some list of vectors.
C4. Why is the set of vectors with first entry equal to \(1\) not a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)?
C5. Give a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) that is not in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)\}\).






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. \(v=\alpha a+\beta b\) (any equivalent wording).
C2. Yes. \((3,3)=3\cdot(1,1)\).
C3. True (in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) every subspace has a basis, hence is a span). For this course it is enough to know that the subspaces we meet are spans.
C4. It does not contain \(0\) (first entry would be \(0\)), or equivalently it is not closed under scaling.
C5. Example: \((1,0)\), or \((2,1)\), or any vector not a multiple of \((1,2)\).

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(1,1)\).

Is \(\{a,b\}\) independent? Does it span \(\mathbb{R}^2\)?
Can every \(v=(v_1,v_2)\) be written uniquely as \(\alpha a+\beta b\)? (Try \(v=(2,3)\).)

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Fill in
A basis of a subspace \(V\) is a list of vectors that is both

\(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) (no redundancy), and
a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) set for \(V\) (every vector in \(V\) is a linear combination of the list).

What a basis accomplishes: every \(v\in V\) has coefficients (coordinates) with respect to the basis — a unique recipe \(v=\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k\).
The dimension of \(V\) is the number of vectors in \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of \(V\). (All bases of \(V\) have the same length.)
Examples:

\(\dim\mathbb{R}^n=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) (standard basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\)).
A line through the origin through a nonzero \(a\) has dimension \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
A plane through the origin spanned by two independent vectors has dimension \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).

An orthonormal list \(q_1,\ldots,q_k\) satisfies \(q_i^{\mathsf{T}}q_j=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) if \(i\neq j\), and \(\lVert q_i\rVert=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
For an orthonormal basis of a subspace, the coefficients of \(v\) are especially simple: \[
\beta_i = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}
\] (inner products — no linear system to solve). That is why orthonormal coordinates are convenient for measurement and reconstruction.

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Worked in class
W1. Basis or not? For each list, is it a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)? If not, say whether it fails independence, spanning, or both.

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((1,1),\ (2,2)\)
\((1,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,1)\)
\((1,1)\) alone

W2. Dimension. Let \(V=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0),(2,4,0),(0,0,1)\}\). Find a basis of \(V\) and \(\dim V\).
W3. Vocabulary drill. Fill each blank with one of: linear combination, span, subspace, independent, dependent, basis, dimension.

\(\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\) is always a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(c=2a-b\), then \(\{a,b,c\}\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
A \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(V\) is an independent spanning list for \(V\).

W4. Orthonormal check. Which of these pairs in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is orthonormal?

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((1,1)/\sqrt{2},\ (1,-1)/\sqrt{2}\)
\((1,0),\ (1,1)\)

W5. Orthonormal coordinates. Let \(q_1=(1,0)\) and \(q_2=(0,1)\) (standard basis — already orthonormal). For \(v=(3,-2)\), what are \(\beta_1=q_1^{\mathsf{T}}v\) and \(\beta_2=q_2^{\mathsf{T}}v\)? Check \(v=\beta_1 q_1+\beta_2 q_2\).
W6 (time permitting). Gram–Schmidt idea. From independent \(a_1=(1,1)\) and \(a_2=(1,0)\), form \(q_1=a_1/\lVert a_1\rVert\), then subtract from \(a_2\) its projection onto \(q_1\), and normalize. (Board sketch only.)

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Check yourself
C1. A basis of a subspace is a list that is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) and \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C2. \(\dim\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)\}=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
C3. True or false: every spanning list for \(V\) is a basis of \(V\).
C4. If \(\{q_1,q_2\}\) is orthonormal and \(v=\beta_1 q_1+\beta_2 q_2\), then \(\beta_1=\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C5. Why are orthonormal coordinates nicer than coordinates in a skewed basis like \((1,0),\ (1,1)\)?






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. independent and spanning (for that subspace).
C2. \(2\)
C3. False. Spanning lists can be dependent (too many vectors); a basis cannot.
C4. \(\beta_1=q_1^{\mathsf{T}}v\)
C5. Coefficients are inner products (no \(2\times 2\) solve); lengths and angles stay easy because the basis vectors are unit and orthogonal.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Course Description (Catalog Description)
Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
Division: Lower Division.
Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs.
Instruction Mode: Face to face only.
Prerequisite: (MATH 101 and MATH 101T) or MATH 102 or ALEKS PPL assessment score 78–100 or appropriate high school coursework. All prerequisite courses must be passed with a grade of C− or higher. See Math Placement and ALEKS PPL for details.
Note: if you plan to use MATH 107 as a prerequisite for another MATH, DATA, or STAT course, you must have a grade of C− or better in this course.

Course Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily learning objectives for each meeting are on Lectures.


General Education & Institutional Learning Outcomes
This course fulfills Lower Division General Education Area 2 (Mathematics) and supports Cal Poly Humboldt’s Institutional Learning Outcomes related to quantitative reasoning, critical thinking, and communication.

Late or Missed Work Policies
The policies for late or missed work are as follows:

Lecture attendance is required, but I know that sometimes you will need to miss class due to illness or other emergencies. Each student may miss up to 10 lecture days without penalty and without contacting me. Reserve these days for emergencies. In my experience, it is rare for a student to succeed if they regularly miss class or are absent for more than two weeks, so if you find yourself in that situation, please communicate with me and your advisor so we can help you find a solution.
Quizzes are in the first 10 minutes of class. The lowest two quiz scores are dropped. If you must miss a quiz due to illness or another emergency, please contact me to arrange a makeup.
Labs are due on the dates on the schedule. After a week, late labs are not accepted.
Capstone work is due on the dates on the schedule. Late project work cannot be turned in due to the end of the semester and course grades being due. If you are unable to complete the project in time, you should consider whether your situation is such that an Incomplete grade is appropriate. This would give you more time to complete the course.
Midterms and the final exam are required. If you need to miss a midterm due to illness or another emergency, communicate with me as soon as possible to reschedule.

Note: Technology issues (internet access, device failure, software problems) are not automatically considered valid excuses for late or missed work; students are expected to plan accordingly.


AI Policy
Much of your course grade will be based on work you produce in class (quizzes and exams) without having the option of using AI as a resource.
Outside of in-class assessments, you may use AI, such as NotebookLM or ChatGPT, to help you learn the material or to get unstuck on labs or the capstone.
For work that you do at home that is turned in for a grade I have two requirements:

If you used AI, acknowledge this briefly in the document (you don’t need to state in detail how you used AI or give your prompts, just the name of the AI service you used).
Be responsible for the correctness and appropriateness of all (AI-assisted or not) materials you turn in.

I may use AI to assist me in my delivery of the course material, such as asking whether an assignment is appropriate for a college-level course or whether the wording of a quiz question could be improved. I will not use AI to grade your work or use an AI detection tool to check your work.
